passage: Coach's note, Tuesday. Tanvir stayed behind after nets and asked if he could talk. "Sir, I want to speak to Omkar," Tanvir said, "but he's the captain and everyone likes him. If I go first, won't I look desperate?" I asked what Tanvir wanted to say. "That the catch on Saturday was really good." I said that sounded honest, and simple honest lines often work better than clever ones. The worry, I think, is about being judged, not about Omkar. Tanvir practised it once, then took a breath and walked over. Omkar said, "Thanks, that ball was slippery!" and they talked kit bags until the bus.

qa.q: What did Tanvir want to say to Omkar?
qa.a: That the catch on Saturday was really good.

qa.q: What was Tanvir afraid of when asking to speak to the captain?
qa.a: Looking desperate by talking first to someone everyone likes, a fear of being judged.

qa.q: What did the coach do that helped Tanvir decide to speak?
qa.a: The coach asked what Tanvir wanted to say and pointed out that the honest, simple line was a good one.

qa.q: How did Omkar respond to Tanvir?
qa.a: Omkar answered warmly, saying thanks and that the ball was slippery, and they chatted until the bus, so the first line was welcome.

grounding: A teenager fears talking first to a popular peer looks desperate, and a simple honest opener works.

passage:
Friday, 9 pm. I wrote three opening lines for Vikas on the back of my rough copy. One was a pun. One was about the physics test. One was so clever I crossed it out because it didn't even sound like me. All I could think was, what if he thinks I'm trying too hard? I kept picturing Vikas walking away. Then at the corridor stall today I just said, "Hey, I really liked your poster." Nothing else. Vikas smiled and said, "Thanks, I worked on it all week." That was it. I walked home surprised how ordinary it felt. Maybe simple was always enough.
Lalit

qa.q: What did Lalit say to Vikas at the corridor stall?
qa.a: "Hey, I really liked your poster."

qa.q: What was Lalit worried about while writing the opening lines?
qa.a: That trying too hard would look bad, and picturing Vikas walking away, a fear of being judged.

qa.q: What did Lalit decide at the stall, and why did it work?
qa.a: Lalit dropped the clever lines and said one honest thing about the poster, which was easy to answer.

qa.q: What might Vikas be feeling when hearing about the poster?
qa.a: Pleased that the work was noticed. Vikas smiled and said it had taken all week.

grounding: A teenager worries talking first to someone will look desperate, and finds a simple honest opener works.

passage:
"Damini, okay, I have to tell you what happened with Rehaan. You know how I've been planning to talk to him for, like, a month?
I had all these lines ready. Something clever about his band T-shirt. Something about the physics test. I thought if I said anything simple, it'd look desperate, like I'm a fangirl. And everyone would see.
So I kept waiting for the perfect moment. There isn't one, by the way.
Yesterday he was at the library, reading the same poetry book I read last year. And I just walked over, heart going crazy, and said, 'Hi. I read that one. The last poem made me cry.' That's it. Not clever at all.
He looked up and said, 'Wait, me too. The one about the train?' And we talked for twenty minutes.
I'm Zeenat, and I'm never planning a clever line again."

qa.q: What book was Rehaan reading in the library?
qa.a: The same poetry book Zeenat read last year.

qa.q: What was Zeenat afraid of before talking to Rehaan?
qa.a: Zeenat was afraid of looking desperate and of being judged if she said anything simple.

qa.q: Why did Zeenat's simple opener work better than a clever line?
qa.a: It was honest and real, sharing a feeling about the poem, which gave Rehaan an easy, genuine way to respond.

qa.q: How might Rehaan have felt when Zeenat mentioned crying at the last poem?
qa.a: He probably felt surprised and connected, since it made him cry too.

grounding: Shows a teenager afraid that talking first to a crush looks desperate, and finding that a simple honest opener works better than clever ones.

passage:
Monday: Bhavna had wanted to talk to Ira, the most popular girl in Class 10, since the term began. That night she wrote three clever openers in her notebook. She didn't use any.
Wednesday: Bhavna tried one at the canteen. "So, are you, like, the queen of this school or what?" Ira blinked. "Um. No?" and turned back to her friends. Bhavna's face burned all through maths. She was sure everyone had noticed.
The next Tuesday: Ira dropped her pen near Bhavna's desk. Bhavna picked it up and, without thinking, said, "Hi. Your handwriting is really neat. Mine is terrible." Ira laughed. "Thanks. I had to practise because my teacher in Class 5 was so strict." They talked all through break about strict teachers.

qa.q: What did Bhavna say at the canteen on Wednesday?
qa.a: She said, 'So, are you, like, the queen of this school or what?'

qa.q: What was Bhavna feeling after the canteen line flopped?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and humiliated, her face burning all through maths, sure everyone had noticed.

qa.q: Which opener worked, and why?
qa.a: The simple honest compliment about Ira's handwriting worked, because it was genuine and easy to answer, unlike the clever-sounding line.

qa.q: How might Ira have seen Bhavna's first line?
qa.a: Ira was probably confused or put off, not sure how to answer a question that sounded like a joke.

grounding: Shows a teenager afraid of looking desperate talking to a popular peer, whose clever opener fails while a simple honest one works.

passage:
"Lavanya, beta, stop rehearsing in the mirror," said Nikita masi, laughing from the doorway. "Sit. When I was sixteen, there was a boy in my tuition class, Sameer. Everyone liked him. I wanted to talk to him so badly, but I was sure that if I spoke first, the whole class would think I was chasing him.
For two months I planned lines. Jokes. Clever things about the maths teacher. I never said any.
Then one day it rained, and we were both stuck under the tuition centre's tin roof. I was so nervous I just said, 'I don't have an umbrella either.' That's all. He laughed and said, 'We can run for it together.' We did, and we were friends for years.
The clever lines never mattered. Say something true and simple."

qa.q: What did young Nikita say under the tin roof?
qa.a: She said, 'I don't have an umbrella either.'

qa.q: What was young Nikita afraid of for two months?
qa.a: She was afraid that speaking first would make the whole class think she was chasing Sameer.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Nikita masi's story?
qa.a: Being stuck under the tin roof in the rain, when she said something simple and true instead of a planned line.

qa.q: How might Sameer have seen Nikita's simple remark?
qa.a: He probably found it natural and friendly, which is why he laughed and suggested running together.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling how her fear of looking desperate held her back, and a simple honest opener worked better than clever ones.

passage: The last bell before the Diwali break would ring in six minutes, and Charu, the basketball captain, was packing up two benches away. Mahima had spent the whole period drafting openers in her head. "Hey, great shot on Friday" sounded fake. "So, basketball, huh?" sounded worse. Everyone would see her walking over. They'd think she was trying too hard. Four minutes. Charu zipped her bag. Mahima's hands were sweating. Two minutes. She stood up and said the only true thing she had: "Hi. I want to try for the team after the break, but I don't know how trials work." Charu looked up and smiled. "Oh, nice! Mondays at seven. I'll tell Coach." The bell rang. Nobody had even looked.

qa.q: When are the basketball trials?
qa.a: They are on Mondays at seven.

qa.q: What was Mahima worried about as she drafted openers?
qa.a: She was anxious that walking over would make her look desperate, as if everyone would judge her for trying too hard.

qa.q: Why did Mahima's final opener work?
qa.a: It was simple and honest, saying what she wanted and asking a real question, so Charu could answer easily.

qa.q: How did Charu seem to see Mahima's approach?
qa.a: She seemed pleased rather than judging, and offered to tell Coach.

grounding: Shows a teenager fearing that talking first to a popular peer will look desperate, then finding a plain, honest opener works.
